questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews four portal messages that arrived overnight. Which client should the nurse contact first?
options: The client with asthma who uses the rescue inhaler every 2 hours and cannot finish sentences.
The client with osteoarthritis whose insurance copay for physical therapy increased this month.
The client with multiple sclerosis in remission who asks whether a beginner yoga class is safe.
The client with hypertension who missed yesterday's visit because the bus route changed.
optionRationales: Correct. Frequent rescue use with speech-limiting dyspnea signals an acute exacerbation and a possible airway and breathing threat.
Incorrect. A cost barrier needs a resource response, but it is not an immediate physiologic threat.
Incorrect. This is a reasonable wellness question from a stable client and can be answered after urgent needs.
Incorrect. Transportation is a real access barrier to address, but it can wait until the unstable client is assessed.
questions.rationale: When several clients have chronic conditions, the priority is the one whose current findings show acute change threatening airway, breathing, or circulation. Needing a rescue inhaler every 2 hours and being unable to finish sentences is an acute exacerbation layered on chronic asthma. Social-determinant problems such as cost and transportation matter and need follow-up the same day, but they do not outrank a breathing threat. The tempting error is to pick the access barrier because missed care feels urgent; it is important, not emergent.
questions.takeaway: Chronic illness can flare acutely; a current breathing threat outranks access and wellness concerns.
questions.hintContent: Look for the message describing a change from the client's baseline that affects breathing.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply ABCs: when only one option describes a physiologic threat, it outranks psychosocial and access needs.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client recovering from a hip fracture needs one-person assistance for transfers and toileting. Discharge home is ordered for this afternoon. The client's daughter says, “I work 12-hour night shifts all week, and there is no one else who can help during the day.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider and case manager that daytime help is not in place.
Give the daughter a list of home-care agencies to call after discharge.
Teach the daughter safe transfer technique before she leaves for work today.
Reassure the daughter that her mother's independence will return quickly.
optionRationales: Correct. A caregiving gap makes the discharge plan unsafe, so the team must revise it before the client leaves.
Incorrect. Deferring the gap until after discharge leaves the client without help when care begins.
Incorrect. Teaching does not solve the hours when no helper will be present, so the plan stays unsafe.
Incorrect. This is false reassurance and ignores the identified need for hands-on help.
questions.rationale: A discharge plan is only safe if the client's care needs can actually be met at home. This client needs hands-on help for transfers and toileting, and the daughter has just identified that no one is available during the day. That is a safety problem to escalate before discharge, which is why notifying the provider and case manager comes first. Teaching transfers is tempting because the daughter is willing, but willingness and skill do not cover the hours she is at work.
questions.takeaway: When caregiver capacity cannot meet the client's needs, escalate before discharge rather than teaching around the gap.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether any option actually changes who will be present during the day.
questions.hintStrategy: When a plan is unsafe, choose the action that stops or revises the plan over actions that proceed with it.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse, “Insulin got too expensive, so I've been taking half my dose to make it last.” Today the client reports nausea and increased thirst, and the fingerstick glucose is 348 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Refer the client to social work for a medication assistance program.
Teach the client the complications of skipping prescribed insulin doses.
Review the client's grocery budget and usual daily meal pattern.
Assess the client's current status further and notify the provider.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The cost barrier needs a referral, but the current hyperglycemia and symptoms must be addressed first.
Incorrect. More teaching does not fix the cost barrier or the immediate physiologic change.
Incorrect. Nutrition and budget assessment can follow once the acute problem is managed.
Correct. Marked hyperglycemia with new symptoms is an immediate physiologic concern requiring assessment and provider notification.
questions.rationale: Social determinants often explain why a physiologic problem developed, but the nurse still addresses immediate safety first. A glucose of 348 mg/dL with nausea and thirst suggests worsening hyperglycemia that needs further assessment and prompt provider notification. The social work referral is the most tempting answer because it fixes the root cause, and it should happen during this same visit, just not before the client's current condition is managed. Lecturing about complications also misses that the problem is cost, not knowledge.
questions.takeaway: Address the acute physiologic problem first, then the social barrier that caused it.
questions.hintContent: Separate the reason the problem happened from what the client needs right now.
questions.hintStrategy: When an option fixes the root cause and another addresses current physical risk, physical risk usually comes first.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: An older adult with long-standing osteoarthritis is admitted for knee pain. Today the client cannot recall being in the hospital and keeps calling the nurse by her late sister's name. The son says, “She's just getting older and slowing down.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assess vital signs and cognition and compare them with her baseline.
Reorient the client and place a calendar where she can see it.
Ask the son how long his mother has had memory problems at home.
Document the confusion as expected for an older adult with chronic pain.
optionRationales: Correct. Acute confusion is a red-flag change from baseline that requires prompt assessment regardless of age or chronic diagnosis.
Incorrect. Reorientation is supportive but does not identify the cause of new confusion.
Incorrect. History is useful, but the new change today must be assessed directly and promptly.
Incorrect. Acute confusion is not a normal part of aging and should not be normalized.
questions.rationale: A long-standing diagnosis does not explain a new change in function, and acute confusion is a red flag that requires prompt assessment. Comparing vital signs and cognition with the client's baseline helps identify possible causes such as infection, hypoxia, or medication effects. Asking the son about history is tempting because it gathers data, but it delays assessing the client in front of you. Reorientation and documentation are reasonable later, not as the first response to an unexplained change.
questions.takeaway: New confusion is never ‘just aging’; assess the client against baseline right away.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether the change is chronic or new today.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you implement; choose direct client assessment over secondhand information when a change is new.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: During an intake visit, a client says, “Every clinic I've been to treats me like I'm not worth their time. Why should I trust this place?” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Our staff are trained to treat every client exactly the same way.”
“Would you like me to schedule you with a different provider today?”
“Let's focus on today's visit so we can get your care started.”
“That sounds painful. Can you tell me about what happened before?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This defends the clinic and dismisses the client's experience rather than exploring it.
Incorrect. Offering a change before understanding the concern is premature problem-solving.
Incorrect. Redirecting away from the concern blocks trust and may lead to disengagement.
Correct. Acknowledging the feeling and inviting the client's story builds trust and identifies the access barrier.
questions.rationale: Repeated discriminatory care experiences are a trust and access barrier, and the nursing response is to listen, validate, and then advocate for respectful care. An empathic acknowledgment followed by an open-ended question invites the client to explain what happened and what would help. Defending the clinic is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds reassuring, but it implicitly tells the client the concern is unfounded. Offering a new provider or redirecting to the visit skips the assessment the client's statement calls for.
questions.takeaway: When a client describes discriminatory care, listen and validate before defending or problem-solving.
questions.hintContent: Think about what builds trust with someone who expects to be dismissed.
questions.hintStrategy: In therapeutic communication items, eliminate options that defend, redirect, or solve before the client's concern is explored.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A client is brought to the emergency department after slipping on a loose rug at home. The client reports severe right hip pain, and the right leg appears shortened. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask about rugs, lighting, and other hazards in the client's home.
Teach the family how to secure rugs and clear walking paths at home.
Refer the client to a community fall-prevention program.
Assess pain, circulation, and sensation in the affected leg.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Home hazard assessment supports future prevention but does not address the current injury.
Incorrect. Prevention teaching is appropriate later, after the acute injury is stabilized.
Incorrect. A referral addresses future risk, not the immediate injury and its complications.
Correct. A suspected fracture requires immediate assessment of pain and neurovascular status.
questions.rationale: Injury care has two layers: managing the injury that happened and preventing the next one. Severe hip pain with a shortened leg suggests a fracture, so the immediate priority is assessing pain, circulation, and sensation in the affected limb. Asking about home hazards is the tempting answer because the cause is obvious and prevention matters, but it belongs after the client is stabilized. Teaching and community referrals likewise focus on future risk.
questions.takeaway: Treat the current injury first; prevention of the next injury comes after stabilization.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether each option addresses what has already happened or what might happen later.
questions.hintStrategy: Acute and unstable problems outrank prevention; choose the option that assesses the current injury.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: At a first prenatal visit, a 24-year-old client says she has been sleeping in her car for two weeks and often skips meals because she has no money for food. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask where the client will sleep tonight and contact social work now.
Teach the client which foods provide the most nutrition per dollar.
Give the client a written handout about prenatal vitamins and diet.
Schedule a follow-up visit in four weeks to reassess the client's food intake.
optionRationales: Correct. Lack of shelter and food is an immediate safety need, so the nurse assesses tonight's plan and connects resources now.
Incorrect. Teaching cannot create money or shelter, so it does not address the most basic barrier.
Incorrect. A handout ignores the lack of food and a safe place to store supplies.
Incorrect. Waiting a month leaves an urgent housing and food gap unaddressed.
questions.rationale: Social determinants such as housing and food access can make any teaching plan impossible to carry out. Sleeping in a car and skipping meals during pregnancy are basic safety and nutrition needs, so the first step is to clarify tonight's situation and connect the client with social work the same day. Nutrition-per-dollar teaching is tempting because it sounds practical, but it still assumes the client has money and a place to store food. Delaying follow-up for a month leaves the barrier untouched.
questions.takeaway: Teaching alone cannot solve a lack of food or shelter; match the barrier to a resource now.
questions.hintContent: Identify the most basic need the client described.
questions.hintStrategy: Use Maslow: shelter and food come before knowledge and long-term planning.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client who uses a wheelchair after a spinal cord injury says, “My wife does everything for me now. I feel useless.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Your wife clearly loves you and is glad to help with your care.”
“Many people with spinal cord injuries feel this way at first.”
“I will arrange a counseling referral so you can talk about this.”
“What would you most like to be able to do for yourself again?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This offers reassurance that dismisses the client's feelings about his changed role.
Incorrect. Generalizing minimizes the client's experience and does not explore what matters to him.
Incorrect. A referral may help later, but it passes the concern on without first exploring it.
Correct. Exploring the client's priorities supports participation and identifies roles he wants to regain.
questions.rationale: Illness and injury change family roles, and preserving the client's participation and independence is part of nursing care. Asking what the client would most like to do for himself explores his priorities and can guide therapy, adaptive equipment, and role adjustments with his wife. Reassuring him that his wife is happy to help is the tempting answer, but it reinforces the dependence he is grieving. A counseling referral may be appropriate later, but it should not replace the nurse's own exploration.
questions.takeaway: When a client feels role loss, explore what independence and roles matter to them.
questions.hintContent: Think about which response keeps the focus on the client's own goals.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic communication, favor open-ended exploration over reassurance, generalizing, or referral.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A client with HIV has an undetectable viral load and stable CD4 counts. The client says, “Since my partner died, I haven't left the house in weeks. I don't really see the point anymore.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Point out that the laboratory results show the client is doing very well.
Suggest that the client join a local grief support group next week.
Ask the client directly whether they are having thoughts of suicide.
Schedule a grief counseling appointment for the coming month.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Physical stability does not measure emotional wellness and dismisses the client's distress.
Incorrect. Support may help later, but the statement first requires a safety assessment.
Correct. “I don't see the point” after a major loss requires direct assessment of suicide risk before other plans.
Incorrect. Delaying the response leaves a possible safety risk unassessed.
questions.rationale: Wellness is multidimensional, and normal laboratory values cannot measure emotional or social well-being. This client describes isolation and hopelessness after a loss, and “I don't see the point” is a possible warning sign that requires a direct question about suicidal thoughts. Asking directly does not increase risk and is the safety step that determines what comes next. Support groups and counseling are tempting because they address grief, but they should follow, not replace, the safety assessment.
questions.takeaway: Hopeless statements require a direct suicide-risk question before planning support.
questions.hintContent: Listen for a statement that may signal a safety risk rather than only sadness.
questions.hintStrategy: When a psychosocial item contains a possible safety threat, assess safety first.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A 29-year-old client has had fatigue and joint aches for three months. Initial blood work was normal. The client says, “The doctor found nothing wrong, so maybe I'm imagining this.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Your symptoms are real and still deserve ongoing assessment.”
“A normal result usually means the symptoms will soon go away.”
“Without abnormal results, there is no illness to treat right now.”
“Stress often causes symptoms that do not show up on tests.”
optionRationales: Correct. Illness is the person's experience and deserves assessment even before a disease is identified.
Incorrect. A normal initial test does not predict resolution and may falsely reassure the client.
Incorrect. This confuses illness with disease and dismisses the client's experience.
Incorrect. This assumes a cause without assessment and can make the client feel dismissed.
questions.rationale: Disease refers to structural or functional pathology, while illness is the person's experience of feeling unwell. A client can have a genuine illness experience before any disease is identified, so normal initial results should not end the assessment. Attributing the symptoms to stress is the tempting answer because it offers an explanation, but it assigns a cause that has not been assessed. The accurate response validates the experience and supports continued evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Illness can exist before disease is found; do not dismiss symptoms because one test is normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall which term describes pathology and which describes the person's experience.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that dismiss the client or assume a cause that has not been assessed.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A client treated for lymphoma says, “My scans are clear and I feel great. I'm cured, so I'm canceling my follow-up appointments.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Clear scans mean the lymphoma is gone, so follow-up is optional.”
“You should keep seeing the oncologist only if your symptoms return.”
“Feeling great is a sign that a relapse is very unlikely for you.”
“Remission means disease signs are gone, but monitoring continues.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Remission does not necessarily mean cure, and monitoring remains important.
Incorrect. Waiting for symptoms delays detection of a possible relapse.
Incorrect. Feeling well does not rule out relapse; that is why monitoring continues.
Correct. Remission is lessening or disappearance of disease signs and does not guarantee cure, so follow-up is still needed.
questions.rationale: Remission means symptoms or signs of disease lessen or disappear; it does not necessarily mean cure. Relapse is the return of disease after improvement, and follow-up visits are how it is detected early. Suggesting follow-up only when symptoms return is tempting because it seems to respect the client's choice, but it delays detection. The best response celebrates the improvement while correcting the misunderstanding.
questions.takeaway: Remission is not the same as cure; ongoing monitoring detects relapse.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish what remission means from what cure means.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client states a misconception that affects safety, choose the option that corrects it accurately.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A nurse precepting a student reviews the student's notes about the health-illness continuum. Which statement by the student indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “A client with a chronic disease can still improve their level of wellness.”
“I should ask clients what being healthy means to them personally.”
“A client who feels well may still have a disease that needs screening.”
“A client's place on the continuum is fixed once a diagnosis is made.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This statement is accurate; wellness can improve while a chronic condition persists.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; wellness is defined by the client's priorities.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; asymptomatic disease is possible.
Correct. This needs correction; the continuum describes ongoing movement, not a permanent label.
questions.rationale: The health-illness continuum describes movement between greater wellness and greater illness over time, not a label assigned at diagnosis. A person with a chronic disease can still improve sleep, relationships, activity, or independence, and a person who feels well may have asymptomatic disease. The student's statement that position is fixed after diagnosis contradicts this dynamic view. The statement about asymptomatic disease may tempt students who think ‘feeling well’ means ‘healthy,’ but it is accurate.
questions.takeaway: The health-illness continuum is a moving picture, not a permanent label.
questions.hintContent: Look for the statement that treats health as static.
questions.hintStrategy: In ‘needs further teaching’ items, find the one false statement; the other options are accurate.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client recently discharged after pneumonia has not used the patient portal to view follow-up instructions. The client says, “I don't have internet at home, and the medical words confuse me.” Which nursing action best addresses this barrier?
options: Send a second portal message with a more detailed explanation.
Ask a relative to log into the portal on the client's behalf.
Arrange phone follow-up with plain-language printed instructions.
Teach the client how to download the portal application on a phone.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client cannot access the portal, so a longer message does not reach them.
Incorrect. This bypasses the client's preference and privacy without first asking what they want.
Correct. This removes the internet barrier and uses plain language to address the literacy concern.
Incorrect. The client has no home internet, and the medical language would remain confusing.
questions.rationale: Not using a portal can reflect lack of internet, lack of a device, or difficulty reading medical language, all of which are social determinants rather than lack of interest. This client names both an access barrier and a literacy barrier, so the best plan changes the communication channel and simplifies the language. Teaching the client to download the app is tempting because it seems empowering, but it does not solve the lack of internet or the confusing wording. Involving a relative without asking the client also skips consent and privacy.
questions.takeaway: Match the communication method to the client's actual access and literacy.
questions.hintContent: Count how many barriers the client named, then find the option that addresses all of them.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that directly removes the stated barrier rather than one that adds more of the same.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A nurse arranged a transportation program for a client who missed three appointments because of bus schedule changes. Which finding best shows the intervention was effective?
options: The client attended the next visit using the arranged ride.
The referral to the transportation program was placed in the chart.
The client stated understanding of why the visits are important.
The nurse documented the transportation barrier in the care plan.
optionRationales: Correct. Attending the appointment shows the barrier was actually removed and the goal was met.
Incorrect. Placing a referral is a nursing action, not evidence that the barrier was resolved.
Incorrect. Knowledge was not the barrier, so verbal understanding does not show the plan worked.
Incorrect. Documenting the barrier records the problem but does not show it was resolved.
questions.rationale: Evaluation compares what actually happened with the goal. The goal here was attending care despite a transportation barrier, so the strongest evidence is that the client attended the next visit using the arranged ride. Placing the referral is the tempting answer because it is a completed task, but a referral placed is an intervention, while a successful connection is an outcome. The client's verbal understanding is also weak evidence because knowledge was never the problem.
questions.takeaway: A referral placed is an action; a barrier actually removed is the outcome.
questions.hintContent: Ask which option describes something the client did, not something the nurse did.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, choose the observable client outcome over nurse activities or verbal statements.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
