questions.stem: A 46-year-old landscaper reports ringing in his ears after work and says coworkers have to repeat themselves. He uses leaf blowers and mowers daily. Which response by the nurse best supports injury prevention?
options: “You should have been wearing hearing protection all along.”
“Hearing usually declines with age, so this may not be work related.”
“Tell me about the noise at work and what protection is available.”
“Let's schedule a hearing aid fitting so you can hear coworkers.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This assigns blame and can make the client less willing to discuss exposures.
Incorrect. This dismisses a likely occupational exposure and misses a prevention opportunity.
Correct. Asking about exposure and equipment without blame identifies risk and options for safer conditions.
Incorrect. This jumps to treatment before assessing the exposure that is causing the injury.
questions.rationale: Injury can result from repeated exposure as well as a single event, and repeated loud noise can gradually damage hearing. Effective prevention starts with asking about work, activity, and protective equipment without assigning blame, so the nurse can identify risk and support safer conditions. Attributing the change to age is tempting because hearing does decline over time, but this client has a clear occupational exposure. Blaming language and jumping to hearing aids both miss the assessment needed for prevention.
questions.takeaway: Injury includes gradual exposure; ask about exposures and protection without blame.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether hearing damage can come from repeated exposure rather than one event.
questions.hintStrategy: Prefer nonjudgmental assessment questions over blame, dismissal, or premature treatment.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: While completing a wellness assessment, a client says, “I'm not religious, so you can skip the spiritual questions.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “That's fine. Spiritual wellness only applies to people with a faith.”
“Let's move on to your emotional wellness and how you cope with stress.”
“Everyone has some beliefs, so I need to ask which religion you prefer.”
“What gives your life meaning or helps you get through hard days?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Spiritual wellness concerns meaning and purpose and does not require religious practice.
Incorrect. This skips a wellness dimension that can still be assessed in nonreligious terms.
Incorrect. This assumes a religious identity the client has just declined.
Correct. Spiritual wellness is about meaning and purpose, so this question respects the client while completing the assessment.
questions.rationale: Spiritual wellness concerns meaning and purpose and does not require a particular religious practice. Asking what gives life meaning respects the client's statement while still assessing a dimension that can support coping. Moving on to emotional wellness is the tempting answer because it seems respectful, but it leaves out a source of strength that the nurse could build on. Insisting on a religious preference disregards what the client just said.
questions.takeaway: Spiritual wellness is about meaning and purpose, not necessarily religion.
questions.hintContent: Recall what the spiritual dimension of wellness actually assesses.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that respects the client's words and still gathers the needed information.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: An alert client admitted with a new cancer diagnosis has her partner of 15 years at the bedside. The client's brother arrives and says, “I'm her next of kin. Tell me what the doctors found.” Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Share the findings with the brother because he is a blood relative.
Ask the brother to leave until he can provide proof of relationship.
Ask the client privately who she wants to receive health information.
Give both visitors the same update at once so that no one feels excluded.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Being the nearest relative does not entitle someone to information without the client's consent.
Incorrect. This is confrontational and does not determine what the client wants.
Correct. An alert client decides whom she considers family and who is involved in her care.
Incorrect. Sharing without consent violates privacy and may override the client's wishes.
questions.rationale: Nurses ask whom the client considers family and who they want involved rather than assuming the nearest relative is the preferred decision partner. Because the client is alert, she determines who receives her health information, and asking privately lets her answer freely. Sharing with the brother is the tempting answer because ‘next of kin’ sounds authoritative, but it would breach privacy and ignore the client's choice. Updating both visitors equally has the same problem.
questions.takeaway: An alert client decides who is family and who receives information.
questions.hintContent: Consider who holds the right to decide when the client is alert.
questions.hintStrategy: Client autonomy and privacy guide family-involvement questions; ask the client.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 72-year-old client who has had Parkinson disease for 10 years. Which findings require prompt follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Coughing and choking during meals that began this week.
A resting hand tremor the client has had for several years.
Confusion about the day and place that started this morning.
A slow, shuffling gait with consistent safe use of a walker.
A fall earlier today in which the client struck their head.
optionRationales: Correct. New swallowing difficulty is a change from baseline and raises aspiration risk.
Incorrect. A long-standing tremor is part of the client's known baseline.
Correct. Acute confusion is a red flag that needs prompt assessment, not attribution to the chronic disease.
Incorrect. This is the client's established pattern with a safety measure in place.
Correct. A fall with head strike is an acute injury requiring prompt assessment.
questions.rationale: A chronic diagnosis does not make every finding expected; the nurse compares current findings with the client's baseline. New choking during meals, new confusion, and a fall with a head strike are acute changes that may signal aspiration risk, an underlying cause of delirium, or injury. The long-standing tremor and the slow gait with consistent walker use are part of this client's known pattern. The common trap is to dismiss new findings as ‘just the Parkinson's,’ which delays assessment.
questions.takeaway: In chronic illness, new changes from baseline need prompt follow-up.
questions.hintContent: Sort findings into ‘known for years’ versus ‘new this week or today.’
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option independently; ask whether it is new, worsening, or dangerous.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A 55-year-old client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes makes several statements during a wellness assessment. Which statements identify strengths the nurse can build on in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: “My sister drives me to every appointment and checks on me.”
“I skip meals near the end of the month when money runs out.”
“I love reading and have already looked up recipes to try.”
“My job doesn't allow breaks to check my blood sugar.”
“Knitting in the evening helps me calm down after a hard day.”
optionRationales: Correct. A reliable support person is a social wellness strength that can support access and follow-through.
Incorrect. This identifies a financial and nutrition concern rather than a strength.
Correct. Interest in learning is an intellectual wellness strength that supports self-management.
Incorrect. This is a career-related barrier to address, not a strength.
Correct. A creative coping practice supports emotional wellness and stress management.
questions.rationale: Assessment across the wellness dimensions identifies strengths as well as concerns, and a strength in one area can support a problem in another. A sister who provides transportation reflects social wellness, interest in recipes reflects intellectual wellness, and knitting to cope reflects creative and emotional wellness. Skipping meals for lack of money and having no work breaks are financial and career barriers that need resources or adaptations. Students sometimes overlook strengths because assessments often focus only on problems.
questions.takeaway: Assess wellness strengths, not just problems, and use them to support the plan.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether each statement helps or hinders the client's ability to manage health.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA, test each option against the question asked; here the question is strengths, not problems.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A community clinic nurse is screening clients for social determinants that may affect their care. Which questions or statements are appropriate for the nurse to use? Select all that apply.
options: “How do you usually get to your appointments?”
“In the past month, have you had trouble getting enough food?”
“Why don't you care enough to come to your visits?”
“What gets in the way of taking this medication as prescribed?”
“You probably can't afford this prescription, can you?”
“May I ask about home and money? It helps us plan care that works.”
optionRationales: Correct. This concrete, neutral question assesses transportation access.
Correct. This specific question assesses food security without judgment.
Incorrect. This blames the client and assumes lack of motivation.
Correct. This open question invites the client to name practical barriers.
Incorrect. This is a leading question that makes an assumption and may embarrass the client.
Correct. Explaining why the nurse asks and requesting permission respects privacy and builds trust.
questions.rationale: Social determinant screening works best with concrete, nonjudgmental questions and a clear explanation of why the nurse is asking. Questions about transportation, food access, and barriers to taking medication invite the client to describe real obstacles. Blaming questions and leading assumptions damage trust and can produce inaccurate answers. The leading question about affordability is tempting because cost is a common barrier, but assuming it for the client is stereotyping rather than assessment.
questions.takeaway: Ask concrete, neutral questions about access, and explain why you are asking.
questions.hintContent: Look for wording that blames, assumes, or leads the client.
questions.hintStrategy: Therapeutic questions are open, specific, and nonjudgmental; eliminate ones that assume the answer.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A public health nurse notes that one neighborhood has twice the rate of emergency visits for asthma as the rest of the county. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess housing conditions such as mold, pests, and indoor smoke.
Assess residents' access to primary care and affordable pharmacies.
Attribute the difference to residents not following asthma instructions.
Partner with community leaders to identify barriers and priorities.
Explain the disparity based on the most common ethnicity in the area.
optionRationales: Correct. Neighborhood and built environment conditions can trigger asthma and drive the disparity.
Correct. Healthcare access and cost affect whether controller medications are obtained and used.
Incorrect. This assumes a motivational cause without assessing barriers and inequities.
Correct. Community partnership identifies local barriers and builds trust for solutions.
Incorrect. Attributing outcomes to a group stereotype ignores the conditions that create disparities.
questions.rationale: A health disparity is a difference in outcomes between groups, and the nursing response is to assess the barriers and inequities that contribute to it. Housing conditions and access to primary care and pharmacies are social determinants that directly affect asthma control. Working with community leaders identifies local priorities and builds trust. Blaming residents or attributing the difference to ethnicity is tempting shorthand, but it relies on stereotypes rather than assessing access and conditions.
questions.takeaway: Address disparities by assessing conditions and access, not by stereotyping groups.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each option examines conditions or blames people.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that assume a cause based on group identity or motivation.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: The spouse of a client recovering from a stroke is learning to help with transfers before discharge. Which findings suggest the spouse may not be able to provide this care safely? Select all that apply.
options: The spouse has a 10-pound lifting restriction after recent back surgery.
The spouse says, “I haven't slept more than four hours a night in weeks.”
The spouse correctly demonstrated a transfer using a gait belt today.
The spouse says, “I'll figure it out at home; I don't need to practice.”
The spouse asks about respite resources for occasional relief.
optionRationales: Correct. A physical limitation may prevent safe transfer assistance.
Correct. Exhaustion is a caregiver capacity concern and may make the plan unsafe.
Incorrect. A correct return demonstration supports the spouse's ability to perform the skill.
Correct. Refusing practice means the skill has not been verified despite willingness.
Incorrect. Seeking respite is a healthy coping step, not a sign of unsafe care.
questions.rationale: A family member's willingness does not prove they can safely perform a skill, so the nurse assesses caregiver capacity as carefully as client symptoms. A lifting restriction, ongoing exhaustion, and refusal to practice each raise doubt about safe transfers at home. A correct return demonstration supports capacity, and asking about respite reflects realistic planning. The respite question is tempting to select because it sounds like the spouse is struggling, but planning for relief is a protective strength.
questions.takeaway: Willingness is not capacity; verify the caregiver's physical ability, energy, and skill.
questions.hintContent: Separate findings that show limits from findings that show healthy planning.
questions.hintStrategy: For each SATA option, ask whether it makes safe care more or less likely.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A nurse precepting a new graduate reviews the graduate's charting about several clients. Which documented interpretations are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Client with untreated high cholesterol who feels well: disease without illness.
Client with unexplained fatigue and normal labs: illness experience needs assessment.
Client with hearing loss after years of loud machinery: not an injury, as there was no event.
Client with stable chronic illness and active social life: wellness is not possible.
Client hurt in a fall from a ladder at work: unintentional injury.
optionRationales: Correct. An asymptomatic condition is disease even when the person feels well.
Correct. Illness is the person's experience and deserves assessment before a diagnosis is found.
Incorrect. Injury can result from repeated exposure, not only from a single sudden event.
Incorrect. Wellness remains possible while a person lives with chronic disease.
Correct. A fall at work is an unintentional injury caused by an event.
questions.rationale: Disease describes pathology, illness describes the person's experience, and injury is damage or loss of function caused by an event or exposure. High cholesterol in a client who feels well is disease without illness, and unexplained fatigue with normal labs is illness that still deserves assessment. Gradual hearing loss from repeated noise is an injury even without a single event, and a ladder fall is an unintentional injury. The tempting error is believing injury always requires one sudden event or that chronic disease rules out wellness.
questions.takeaway: Disease is pathology, illness is experience, and injury can come from an event or repeated exposure.
questions.hintContent: Check each interpretation against the definitions of disease, illness, injury, and wellness.
questions.hintStrategy: Watch for absolute words such as ‘not possible’ or ‘no event’ that make a statement false.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A client who reads at about a third-grade level is learning to take a new blood pressure medication at home. Which teaching strategies should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
options: Use short sentences and everyday words instead of medical terms.
Use pictures or a simple chart to show when to take each dose.
Ask the client to explain in their own words how they will take the pill.
Provide a detailed brochure so the client can review it at home.
Ask, “Do you understand?” at the end of the session.
Limit the session to the two or three most essential points.
optionRationales: Correct. Plain language makes instructions usable for clients with limited literacy.
Correct. Visual aids support understanding when reading is difficult.
Correct. Teach-back verifies understanding rather than assuming it.
Incorrect. Dense written material is hard to use with limited literacy.
Incorrect. A yes/no question often produces agreement without confirming understanding.
Correct. Focusing on key actions prevents overload and improves retention.
questions.rationale: When a client cannot read instructions well, the nurse uses plain language, pictures, and teach-back. Limiting teaching to the most essential points prevents overload, and teach-back confirms what the client will actually do. A detailed brochure is tempting because it seems thorough, but it depends on the reading skill the client lacks. Asking “Do you understand?” invites a polite yes and does not verify learning.
questions.takeaway: For limited literacy, use plain language, pictures, a few key points, and teach-back.
questions.hintContent: Ask which strategies work without depending on reading skill.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching SATA items, favor strategies that verify learning over those that only deliver information.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health, Wellness, Illness & Injury · slides 3–19

questions.stem: A 52-year-old office worker with no activity restrictions says, “I don't see why I need to exercise. I feel fine the way I am.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Here is a walking schedule you can start this week.”
“Inactivity raises your risk of heart disease and diabetes.”
“What are your thoughts about how activity fits your life?”
“Most adults need at least 150 minutes of activity each week.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A schedule fits preparation, not a client who is not yet considering change.
Incorrect. Leading with risk warnings can feel like pressure and may increase resistance.
Correct. Exploring the client's perspective is the stage-matched approach for precontemplation.
Incorrect. Offering a target before exploring beliefs skips the client's current readiness.
questions.rationale: A client who sees no reason to change is in precontemplation, and the stage-matched approach is to explore the client's perspective and offer information with permission. An open question about how activity fits the client's life invites the client's view and can reveal what matters to them. Stating risks is tempting because it is accurate, but leading with warnings often feels like pressure. Schedules and weekly targets belong to later stages, when the client is preparing to act.
questions.takeaway: In precontemplation, explore beliefs before offering plans or targets.
questions.hintContent: Identify the stage of change from the client's own words.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the intervention to the client's readiness, not to the nurse's preferred plan.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client says, “I picked the first of next month to quit vaping, and I downloaded a quit app last night.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Help the client plan first steps and support for the quit day.
Explore what the client likes and dislikes about vaping right now.
Review the long-term lung risks associated with vaping.
Discuss strategies for staying vape-free over the next several months.
optionRationales: Correct. The client is in preparation, so the nurse finalizes resources and concrete first steps.
Incorrect. Exploring ambivalence fits contemplation; this client has already committed to a plan.
Incorrect. More risk information does not move a client who is already preparing to act.
Incorrect. Maintenance planning is premature before the client has begun the change.
questions.rationale: A client who has chosen a date and gathered a resource is in the preparation stage. The best next step is to finalize practical resources and first steps, such as handling cravings on day one and identifying support. Exploring pros and cons is tempting because it is good counseling, but it fits contemplation and would slow a client who is ready. Maintenance strategies come after the behavior has been started and sustained.
questions.takeaway: Preparation calls for concrete first steps and resources, not more persuasion.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the client is still deciding, planning, or already doing.
questions.hintStrategy: Stage-of-change items: identify the stage first, then choose the intervention for that stage.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin mentions starting a ginkgo supplement for memory, which a friend said is “natural and safe.” The client has no signs of bleeding. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Tell the client to stop taking warfarin until the supplement is reviewed.
Reassure the client that natural products rarely affect prescriptions.
Ask the product name, dose, and start date and inform the prescriber.
Document the supplement and plan to discuss it at the next visit.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping a prescribed anticoagulant without the prescriber is unsafe.
Incorrect. ‘Natural’ does not prove safety, and ginkgo may increase bleeding risk with warfarin.
Correct. Gathering details and coordinating review addresses a possible interaction without the nurse changing therapy alone.
Incorrect. A possible interaction with an anticoagulant should be reported now, not deferred.
questions.rationale: Complementary products can interact with medications, and ‘natural’ does not prove a product is safe. Ginkgo may add to warfarin's bleeding risk, so the nurse gathers specific details and coordinates review with the prescriber or pharmacist. Telling the client to stop warfarin is tempting because it seems protective, but changing a prescribed anticoagulant without the prescriber creates its own risk. Deferring to the next visit leaves a possible interaction unaddressed.
questions.takeaway: Ask about supplements without judgment, then coordinate review rather than changing therapy yourself.
questions.hintContent: Think about who should decide whether a prescribed medication is changed.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that gathers data and uses the team instead of acting outside scope.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A client who stopped smoking two months ago tells the nurse, “I smoked three cigarettes at a party Saturday. I've ruined everything.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “What was happening at the party when you decided to smoke?”
“One slip means it is time to choose a new quit date and start over.”
“You should avoid parties for now so this doesn't happen again.”
“Three cigarettes is not enough to cause any real harm to you.”
optionRationales: Correct. Exploring the trigger after a lapse supports revising the plan.
Incorrect. Treating a lapse as total failure ignores two months of progress.
Incorrect. Giving advice before exploring the situation skips assessment of the trigger.
Incorrect. This minimizes the event and misses the chance to plan for future triggers.
questions.rationale: A lapse is a reason to identify triggers and revise the plan, not proof that change is impossible. Asking what was happening at the party helps the client recognize the trigger and plan a response, while two months of abstinence remains real progress. Advising the client to avoid parties is tempting because it is practical, but it skips assessment and may not match the client's life. Restarting from zero or minimizing the event both miss the learning opportunity.
questions.takeaway: After a lapse, explore the trigger and revise the plan; do not treat it as failure.
questions.hintContent: Consider what information the nurse needs before suggesting a solution.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before advising; an open question about the situation comes first.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: At a community health fair, a 58-year-old client says, “I want to start jogging. Lately I've been getting chest tightness when I climb the stairs at work.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Teach the client to start at a slow pace and use the talk test.
Advise the client to see a provider promptly before starting jogging.
Help the client set a SMART goal for a beginning jogging program.
Suggest walking instead of jogging until the chest tightness improves.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Intensity teaching assumes the client is safe to exercise, which is not yet established.
Correct. New exertional chest symptoms require medical evaluation before a wellness exercise plan.
Incorrect. Goal-setting should wait until the exertional symptom has been evaluated.
Incorrect. Lower-intensity exercise still adds exertion before the symptom has been assessed.
questions.rationale: Health promotion builds on safety, and new exertional symptoms require assessment before a wellness exercise plan is started. Chest tightness with stair climbing could signal a cardiac problem, so the client needs prompt provider evaluation. Suggesting walking instead is the tempting answer because it seems like a safer compromise, but it still prescribes exertion for an unexplained symptom. Talk-test teaching and SMART goals are appropriate only after the client is cleared.
questions.takeaway: New exertional symptoms mean evaluation before any exercise plan.
questions.hintContent: Notice the symptom the client mentioned almost in passing.
questions.hintStrategy: When a wellness request contains a red-flag symptom, the red flag takes priority.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with hypertension says, “My health is in God's hands. Whatever happens is what is meant to be.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Your health actually depends mostly on the choices you make.”
“Research has not shown that faith lowers blood pressure readings.”
“Let's set a goal for you to walk 30 minutes every day this week.”
“Tell me more about how your faith guides your health decisions.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This dismisses the client's belief and may damage the therapeutic relationship.
Incorrect. Arguing with a belief is not therapeutic and blocks collaboration.
Incorrect. A plan offered before exploring beliefs ignores the client's perspective.
Correct. Exploring the belief respects the client and can reveal actions the client sees as compatible.
questions.rationale: The client describes an external locus of control, a belief that outcomes depend mainly on outside forces. The nurse first explores the belief, because understanding it can reveal actions the client sees as compatible with faith, such as caring for the body or accepting help from others. Telling the client that health depends on their choices is tempting because it emphasizes agency, but it argues with a deeply held belief and damages trust. Offering a walking plan skips assessment entirely.
questions.takeaway: Explore a client's locus of control and beliefs before building a plan around them.
questions.hintContent: Consider which response invites the client to say more.
questions.hintStrategy: Therapeutic responses explore; eliminate options that argue, correct, or jump to a plan.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client started walking after dinner two weeks ago and says, “It's going well, but when it rains I just skip it, and then I skip the next day too.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Could an indoor option, like walking at the mall, work on rainy days?”
“What would be the benefits of exercising regularly for you?”
“Skipping walks suggests you may not be fully committed to reaching this goal.”
“Keep the same schedule and try to be more disciplined about it.”
optionRationales: Correct. The client is in action, so troubleshooting a specific trigger supports the new behavior.
Incorrect. Exploring benefits fits contemplation; this client has already started.
Incorrect. This blames the client and treats a barrier as lack of motivation.
Incorrect. Repeating the plan without addressing the barrier is unlikely to change the result.
questions.rationale: A client who has begun a new behavior is in the action stage, where support focuses on practice and troubleshooting real triggers. Rain is a predictable barrier, so planning an indoor alternative helps the client keep the routine going. Exploring benefits is tempting because it builds motivation, but it belongs to contemplation and does not solve the rainy-day problem. Blaming commitment or urging discipline ignores the barrier entirely.
questions.takeaway: In the action stage, troubleshoot triggers instead of re-arguing benefits.
questions.hintContent: The client has already started; what kind of help fits that stage?
questions.hintStrategy: When the client names a specific barrier, the best answer usually addresses that barrier directly.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client smokes, sleeps about five hours a night, and rarely exercises. The client asks, “Which one should I work on first?” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Smoking causes the most harm, so that should come first.”
“You should try to change all three at the same time.”
“Which of these feels most important or doable for you now?”
“Let's start with sleep, because it is the easiest habit to change.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The nurse's priority may not match the client's readiness, which reduces success.
Incorrect. Changing several behaviors at once often overwhelms the client.
Correct. Starting with the change the client values and feels ready for supports autonomy and success.
Incorrect. This assumes which change is easiest without asking the client.
questions.rationale: Behavior change is a partnership in which the client supplies priorities and the nurse supplies knowledge and support. Asking which change feels most important or doable lets the client choose a manageable first step, which builds self-efficacy and improves follow-through. Choosing smoking because it causes the most harm is the most tempting answer, but a client who is not ready to quit may make no progress at all. The nurse can still share information about risks once the client's priorities are known.
questions.takeaway: Let the client choose the first change; readiness predicts success better than the nurse's ranking.
questions.hintContent: Consider whose priorities should guide a voluntary behavior change.
questions.hintStrategy: Client autonomy questions favor the response that asks the client rather than deciding for them.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews follow-up notes for four clients enrolled in a health-promotion program. Which client should the nurse contact first?
options: The client who replaced prescribed insulin with cinnamon capsules last week.
The client who uses weekly acupuncture alongside prescribed migraine medication.
The client who walked three of four planned days and wants to add a day.
The client who has not chosen a quit date but is thinking about quitting.
optionRationales: Correct. Replacing prescribed insulin with an unreviewed alternative creates an immediate safety risk.
Incorrect. This is complementary use alongside conventional care and is not urgent.
Incorrect. This client is progressing well and can be supported routinely.
Incorrect. A client in contemplation needs support, but there is no immediate safety threat.
questions.rationale: Complementary practices are used alongside conventional care, while alternative practices replace it. Replacing prescribed insulin with a supplement is an alternative approach that can quickly lead to dangerous hyperglycemia, so this client needs contact first. Acupuncture alongside medication is complementary use and is not a safety concern on its own. The contemplating smoker is tempting because tobacco carries serious risk, but that risk is not immediate in the way stopping insulin is.
questions.takeaway: Replacing prescribed treatment with an unreviewed alternative is a safety concern; complementary use is not.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish therapies used alongside treatment from those used instead of it.
questions.hintStrategy: Prioritize the client whose situation could cause harm soonest.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

rows: Stopped prescribed insulin; taking cinnamon capsules instead since last week.
Acupuncture weekly; continues prescribed migraine medication.
Walked 3 of 4 planned days; wants to add a fifth day.
Thinking about quitting smoking; no quit date yet.

questions.stem: A nurse at a senior center leads a weekly balance class for adults over 70 who have never fallen. A student says, “This is secondary prevention because older adults are at high fall risk.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Yes, because the class targets a group that has higher risk.”
“It is primary prevention, because no fall has occurred yet.”
“It is tertiary prevention, because balance declines with aging.”
“It is secondary prevention, because balance is being screened.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Targeting a higher-risk group does not change the level; timing relative to the condition does.
Correct. The class acts before the target injury occurs, which defines primary prevention.
Incorrect. Tertiary prevention limits the impact of an established condition or injury.
Incorrect. The class trains balance to prevent falls rather than detecting an existing condition.
questions.rationale: Prevention level is determined by the purpose and timing relative to the target condition, not by how risky the population is. A balance class for adults who have never fallen acts before the injury occurs, so it is primary prevention. The student's reasoning is tempting because high-risk groups are often screened, but screening detects an existing condition early, and this class is not detecting anything. If the same class were part of rehabilitation after a fall-related fracture, it would be tertiary.
questions.takeaway: Classify prevention by whether the target condition has occurred, not by the group's risk level.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the target event has already happened for these clients.
questions.hintStrategy: For prevention-level items, name the target condition first, then check its timing.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A school nurse reviews screening results for students. A 15-year-old with no known vision problems fails the eye chart screening and is referred for an eye examination. Which level of prevention does this screening represent?
options: Primary, because the screening helps prevent future vision loss.
Tertiary, because the referral will treat the vision problem.
Secondary, because it detects a possible existing problem.
Primary, because it is offered to all students in the school.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Primary prevention acts before a condition develops; this screening looks for an existing one.
Incorrect. Tertiary prevention limits impact after a condition is established and treated.
Correct. Screening an asymptomatic person to detect a condition early is secondary prevention.
Incorrect. Offering a service to everyone does not make it primary; its purpose is detection.
questions.rationale: Secondary prevention is early detection of a condition that may already exist, commonly through screening. Vision screening identifies a problem in a student who did not know about it, so the referral can lead to early correction. Calling it primary is tempting because the eventual goal is protecting vision, but primary prevention acts before the condition develops, such as protective eyewear. Tertiary prevention would be rehabilitation or managing complications of an established eye condition.
questions.takeaway: Screening asymptomatic people to find a condition early is secondary prevention.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the activity prevents a condition or finds one.
questions.hintStrategy: Focus on the purpose of the activity, not who receives it or its long-range benefit.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 49-year-old client about risk factors for stroke. Which statement by the client indicates an accurate understanding?
options: “Because my mother had a stroke, my lifestyle choices won't matter.”
“I can't change my family history, but I can stop smoking and move more.”
“Since smoking is modifiable, quitting should be easy for me to do.”
“My age is my biggest risk factor, so I'll work on changing that one first.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Family history raises risk but does not cancel the benefit of modifiable changes.
Correct. The client distinguishes nonmodifiable risk from modifiable behaviors that can reduce risk.
Incorrect. Modifiable does not mean easy; context and support influence change.
Incorrect. Age is nonmodifiable and cannot be the focus of a behavior change plan.
questions.rationale: Nonmodifiable risk factors such as age and family history cannot be changed, while modifiable factors such as tobacco use and inactivity can. Inherited risk and modifiable behaviors coexist, so a client with a family history still benefits from changing what can be changed. The statement that quitting should be easy is tempting because it uses the correct term, but modifiable does not mean easy; work, stress, and support all influence change. The statement about age confuses what can be targeted.
questions.takeaway: Modifiable means changeable, not easy; inherited risk does not cancel lifestyle benefit.
questions.hintContent: Sort each risk factor into ‘can change’ or ‘cannot change.’
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation-of-teaching items, the correct answer is the only fully accurate statement.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client says, “I know walking would help my blood pressure, but I never stick with anything. I don't think I can do it.” Which nursing action best builds the client's self-efficacy?
options: Provide research showing how walking lowers blood pressure.
Set a goal of 30 minutes of brisk walking every single day this week.
Explain that most people find it hard to begin an exercise habit.
Agree on a brief first walk the client feels confident completing.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client already believes walking helps; the barrier is confidence, not knowledge.
Incorrect. A demanding first goal risks failure and may further lower confidence.
Incorrect. Normalizing difficulty does not build the client's belief in their own ability.
Correct. Small achievable successes strengthen the belief that one can perform the behavior.
questions.rationale: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can successfully perform a specific action, and it grows through achievable successes. This client already knows walking helps, so the barrier is confidence rather than information. A short first walk the client is confident about creates a success to build on. Presenting research is tempting because it sounds evidence-based, but more facts do not address doubt about personal ability.
questions.takeaway: Build self-efficacy with small, achievable successes, not more information.
questions.hintContent: Identify whether the client lacks knowledge or lacks confidence.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the intervention to the specific barrier the client states.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for a 74-year-old client recovering from pneumonia says, “He needs 150 minutes of activity a week to meet national goals, so I'll walk him 30 minutes today.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “That's right; meeting the national target speeds his recovery.”
“Let's first assess his tolerance and build from his baseline.”
“National goals apply only to healthy people, not hospital clients.”
“Walk him 10 minutes three times today to reach the same total.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A population target does not establish what this client can safely do today.
Correct. Individual assessment determines a safe starting point; population goals do not replace it.
Incorrect. People with illness should be as active as abilities allow; the issue is individualizing, not exclusion.
Incorrect. Splitting the same total still sets activity by a target instead of assessed tolerance.
questions.rationale: Population goals such as national activity targets help communities set direction, but they do not replace individual assessment. A client recovering from pneumonia needs an assessment of tolerance, symptoms, and the clinical plan before activity is set. Splitting the walk into shorter bouts is the tempting answer because it seems safer, but it still starts from the population number rather than this client's baseline. Excluding hospitalized clients from activity goals is also incorrect; they should be as active as their condition allows.
questions.takeaway: A national target is not an exercise prescription; start from the individual's assessed baseline.
questions.hintContent: Consider what should determine the starting dose of activity for one client.
questions.hintStrategy: Prefer ‘assess first’ when an option bases care on a general rule rather than the client.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A community nurse is evaluating a free blood pressure screening program held at local churches. Which measure best shows that the program achieved a meaningful outcome?
options: The number of educational flyers handed out at each event.
The number of people who had their blood pressure checked.
The share of people with high readings who completed follow-up care.
The volunteers' satisfaction ratings collected at the end of each event.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Distributing flyers measures an activity, not a health outcome.
Incorrect. Screening volume shows reach but not whether people with high readings received care.
Correct. Completing follow-up shows that detection led to access to care.
Incorrect. Volunteer satisfaction does not reflect client health outcomes.
questions.rationale: Counting brochures or events measures activity, while measuring whether people can obtain care addresses a more meaningful outcome. A screening program achieves its purpose when people with elevated readings actually connect with follow-up care. The number of people screened is the tempting answer because it shows reach, but detecting high blood pressure without follow-up does not change health. Volunteer satisfaction has value for the program but not for client outcomes.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate programs by whether people obtained care or changed behavior, not by activity counts.
questions.hintContent: Ask which measure reflects what happened to clients after screening.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, choose the client outcome over process measures.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client who works double shifts has been trying to eat more vegetables and says, “I only managed it on my days off.” Which nurse statement is most likely to strengthen the client's motivation?
options: “Why didn't you prepare meals ahead so you could stick to the plan?”
“If you don't change, your cholesterol will keep going up.”
“You made it work on your days off. What helped on those days?”
“I know exactly how hard it is to eat well with a busy job.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A ‘why’ question sounds judgmental and puts the client on the defensive.
Incorrect. Threats tend to increase resistance rather than motivation.
Correct. An affirmation of real effort plus an open question builds on the client's own strategies.
Incorrect. Claiming to know exactly how the client feels is not true empathy and shifts focus to the nurse.
questions.rationale: Motivational communication uses affirmations that identify real effort and open questions that draw on the client's own experience. Recognizing success on days off and asking what helped lets the client identify strategies that might work on workdays. The empathic-sounding statement is tempting, but claiming to know exactly how the client feels is not genuine empathy and redirects attention to the nurse. ‘Why’ questions and threats tend to provoke defensiveness.
questions.takeaway: Affirm real effort and ask what worked; avoid blame, threats, and false empathy.
questions.hintContent: Look for a response that builds on something the client already did well.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options with ‘why’ questions, threats, or claims to know exactly how the client feels.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse writes the goal “The client will eat a healthier diet.” for a 38-year-old client with prediabetes. The client wants to cut back on sweet tea. Which revision best meets SMART-EST criteria?
options: “The client will understand why sugary drinks raise blood glucose by discharge.”
“The client will stop drinking all sweetened beverages of any kind starting tomorrow.”
“The client will follow the recommended diabetic diet as closely as possible.”
“The client will replace two daily glasses of sweet tea with water for one week.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. ‘Understand’ is not directly observable, and the goal does not describe a behavior.
Incorrect. An abrupt, all-or-nothing goal may not be achievable and lacks a review date.
Incorrect. This is vague and not measurable or tailored to the client's chosen change.
Correct. The goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant to the client's choice, and time-bound.
questions.rationale: SMART-EST goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, as well as evidence-based, strategic, and tailored. Replacing two glasses of sweet tea with water for one week names an observable behavior, an amount, and a time frame, and it reflects the change the client chose. Stopping all sweetened drinks is tempting because it is specific, but an abrupt all-or-nothing target may not be achievable and has no review point. Goals based on ‘understanding’ or ‘as closely as possible’ cannot be evaluated.
questions.takeaway: A strong goal names an observable behavior, amount, time frame, and the client's own priority.
questions.hintContent: Check each option for an observable action and a time frame.
questions.hintStrategy: For goal-writing items, eliminate any goal with ‘understand,’ ‘as possible,’ or no time frame.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse in a primary care clinic reviews the day's planned services. Which services are examples of secondary prevention? Select all that apply.
options: A cervical cancer screening test for a woman with no symptoms.
A tetanus booster for a gardener with no current wound.
A depression screening questionnaire at a 6-week postpartum visit.
Cardiac rehabilitation exercise after a recent myocardial infarction.
A blood pressure check for an adult with no known hypertension.
Teaching a new driver to always wear a seat belt.
optionRationales: Correct. Screening an asymptomatic person detects a possible condition early.
Incorrect. Immunization prevents disease before it occurs, which is primary prevention.
Correct. Screening identifies an existing condition early in a client without a diagnosis.
Incorrect. Rehabilitation after established disease is tertiary prevention.
Correct. Screening for undiagnosed hypertension is early detection.
Incorrect. This prevents injury before it occurs, which is primary prevention.
questions.rationale: Secondary prevention detects an existing condition early, commonly through screening in people without a known diagnosis. Cervical cancer screening, postpartum depression screening, and blood pressure checks in adults without hypertension all look for a condition that may already be present. Immunization and seat-belt teaching act before disease or injury occurs, which is primary prevention. Cardiac rehabilitation is tempting because it involves exercise and monitoring, but it limits the impact of established disease, which is tertiary.
questions.takeaway: Secondary prevention = screening and early detection in people without a known diagnosis.
questions.hintContent: For each service, ask whether the target condition might already be present but undetected.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each SATA option on its own by the purpose of the activity.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse is planning care for several clients with established conditions. Which nursing actions represent tertiary prevention? Select all that apply.
options: Arranging speech therapy for a client with aphasia after a stroke.
Teaching a client with type 1 diabetes daily foot checks to prevent ulcers.
Scheduling a screening mammogram for a 50-year-old with no symptoms.
Referring a client with heart failure to a self-management support group.
Giving the HPV vaccine to a healthy 12-year-old.
optionRationales: Correct. Rehabilitation after a stroke restores function after an established condition.
Correct. Teaching complication prevention for an established disease is tertiary prevention.
Incorrect. Screening for early detection in an asymptomatic person is secondary prevention.
Correct. Supporting self-care in established disease reduces complications and preserves function.
Incorrect. Immunization before disease occurs is primary prevention.
questions.rationale: Tertiary prevention reduces complications and restores function after a disease or injury is established. Speech therapy after a stroke, foot-care teaching for diagnosed diabetes, and heart failure self-management support all address conditions that are already present. Screening mammography is secondary prevention because it looks for disease early, and vaccination is primary prevention. Foot-care teaching is easy to misclassify as primary because it is education, but education appears at all three levels; the established diagnosis makes it tertiary.
questions.takeaway: Education can be any level; when the condition is already established, it is tertiary.
questions.hintContent: For each action, check whether the client already has the condition being targeted.
questions.hintStrategy: Do not classify by the type of activity (teaching, exercise); classify by its purpose and timing.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating several clients who want to stop smoking. Which statements indicate the client is in the preparation stage of change? Select all that apply.
options: “I picked June 1 as my quit date and told my family about it.”
“I bought nicotine patches and scheduled a quitline call next week.”
“I've been smoke-free for three weeks, but evenings are tough.”
“I've thought about quitting someday, but I'm not sure I'm ready.”
“I haven't smoked in eight months and rarely think about it.”
optionRationales: Correct. Choosing a date and arranging support are planning steps in preparation.
Correct. Gathering resources for an upcoming change indicates preparation.
Incorrect. The client has started the change, which is the action stage.
Incorrect. Weighing change without a plan reflects contemplation.
Incorrect. Sustaining the behavior for months reflects maintenance.
questions.rationale: Preparation means the person intends to act and is planning practical steps, such as choosing a date and gathering resources. Once the behavior has begun, the client is in action, and sustaining it for months reflects maintenance. Uncertain thoughts about quitting someday indicate contemplation. The three-weeks-smoke-free statement is tempting because the client is still struggling, but the behavior has already started, which defines action.
questions.takeaway: Planning a change is preparation; performing it is action.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether each client is thinking, planning, doing, or sustaining.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each statement into a stage independently; only the planning statements fit.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A client says, “I want to drink less on weekends, but it's how I unwind with friends.” Which nurse statements are therapeutic for this client? Select all that apply.
options: “What do you enjoy about drinking, and what concerns you about it?”
“It sounds like you want to cut back but don't want to lose time with friends.”
“Would it be okay if I shared some information about alcohol and sleep?”
“If you keep drinking like this, you will damage your liver.”
“If you cut back to two drinks, I promise you'll feel much better.”
“Why can't you just find a different way to relax?”
optionRationales: Correct. An open question explores both sides of the client's ambivalence.
Correct. Reflection shows understanding and lets the client clarify.
Correct. Asking permission before giving information respects autonomy.
Incorrect. Threats tend to increase resistance rather than motivation.
Incorrect. Nurses should not promise that a behavior will guarantee a result.
Incorrect. ‘Why’ questions sound judgmental and put the client on the defensive.
questions.rationale: A client weighing change with mixed feelings is in contemplation, where the nurse explores benefits, concerns, and ambivalence. Open questions, reflections, and asking permission before sharing information all support the client's own reasoning. Threats, guarantees, and ‘why’ questions undermine the relationship and tend to increase resistance. The promise of feeling better is tempting because it sounds encouraging, but no behavior guarantees a specific result.
questions.takeaway: Use open questions, reflection, and permission; avoid threats, promises, and ‘why’ questions.
questions.hintContent: Identify the stage of change, then choose techniques that fit ambivalence.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement for blame, pressure, or false guarantees.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: A nurse is beginning a health-promotion plan with a client who wants to be more active. Which actions belong to the assessment phase of the nursing process? Select all that apply.
options: Asking about the client's current activity and daily routine.
Exploring what the client believes will improve their health.
Writing a measurable outcome with a review date.
Asking how ready the client feels to make a change now.
Comparing the client's actual activity with the agreed goal.
Asking who could support the client and what resources are nearby.
optionRationales: Correct. Gathering current habits is assessment.
Correct. Health beliefs are assessed before planning.
Incorrect. Setting the shared outcome is planning.
Correct. Readiness for change is part of assessment.
Incorrect. Comparing results with the goal is evaluation.
Correct. Support and resources are assessed before planning.
questions.rationale: In ADPIE, assessment gathers habits, beliefs, readiness, symptoms, resources, and support. Asking about routine, beliefs, readiness, and support all belong to assessment and shape a plan the client can carry out. Writing a measurable outcome is planning, and comparing actual behavior with the goal is evaluation. The goal-writing option is tempting because it involves the client's data, but it uses assessment findings rather than collecting them.
questions.takeaway: Assess habits, beliefs, readiness, and resources before writing the goal.
questions.hintContent: Match each action to a step of ADPIE.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each option collects new data or uses data already collected.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: At a two-week follow-up, a client met the walking goal on only two of eight planned days. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the client what actually happened on the days the walk was missed.
Identify what helped on the two days the client did walk.
Revise the goal or schedule together based on what was learned.
Tell the client to keep the same goal and try harder next time.
Document the client as nonadherent and close the activity goal.
Recognize the two days of walking as progress toward the goal.
optionRationales: Correct. Exploring what happened identifies barriers to address.
Correct. Successful days reveal strategies the client can build on.
Correct. An unmet goal is assessment data used to revise the plan collaboratively.
Incorrect. Repeating the plan without assessing barriers is unlikely to change the result.
Incorrect. Labeling and closing the goal ends the partnership instead of revising the plan.
Correct. Affirming real progress supports motivation and the therapeutic relationship.
questions.rationale: A plan that was not achieved provides assessment information. The nurse asks what happened, identifies what worked, recognizes the progress that did occur, and revises the goal with the client. Urging the client to try harder is tempting because the goal was reasonable, but it assumes motivation is the problem without assessing barriers. Labeling the client nonadherent and closing the goal damages the relationship and abandons the plan.
questions.takeaway: An unmet goal is data: reassess barriers, affirm progress, and revise together.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether each action learns from the shortfall or ignores it.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluation items favor reassessment and revision over repetition or labeling.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: During a health-promotion visit, a client mentions taking several products and practices along with prescribed medications. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask about the client's use of traditional remedies without judgment.
Ask the pharmacist to review the supplements for possible interactions.
Tell the client to stop all supplements until the next clinic visit.
Record each product's name, dose, and frequency in the health history.
Explain that products labeled natural cannot harm the client.
optionRationales: Correct. Nonjudgmental questions encourage honest disclosure of all therapies.
Correct. Coordinating review identifies interactions with prescribed medications.
Incorrect. Stopping products without review is a unilateral change that may not be needed.
Correct. Specific details allow accurate review and communication with the team.
Incorrect. ‘Natural’ does not prove safety; supplements may interact with medication.
questions.rationale: Nurses ask about supplements, traditional practices, and other therapies without judgment so clients feel safe disclosing them. Recording specific product details and coordinating pharmacist review allows the team to identify interactions. Telling the client to stop everything is tempting because it seems cautious, but it is a unilateral change that disregards the client's practices and may be unnecessary. Reassuring the client that natural products are harmless is inaccurate.
questions.takeaway: Ask, document details, and coordinate review; do not dismiss or unilaterally stop therapies.
questions.hintContent: Think about which actions gather information and use the team.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options containing absolutes such as ‘all’ or ‘cannot harm.’
questions.ref: Module 7 · Health Promotion & Behavior Change · slides 20–37

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client is walking in the hallway with the nurse for the first time since admission. Halfway down the hall, the client says, “I feel dizzy, like I might pass out.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Count the client's radial pulse for one full minute.
Help the client sit down in a nearby chair.
Encourage the client to walk slowly back to the room.
Call for another staff member to bring a wheelchair.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Assessment matters, but the client must be protected from falling first.
Correct. Near-syncope during activity calls for stopping and protecting the client from a fall before assessing.
Incorrect. Continued walking while near-syncopal increases the risk of a fall.
Incorrect. Waiting for equipment leaves the client standing and at risk of falling.
questions.rationale: New dizziness or near-syncope during activity means stopping and assessing, and the first part of stopping is protecting the client from injury. Helping the client sit right away prevents a fall if the client loses consciousness. Taking the pulse is the tempting answer because it is assessment, and assessment usually comes first, but here the immediate safety risk is falling. Once seated, the nurse assesses vital signs and symptoms and reports the change.
questions.takeaway: For near-syncope during activity, stop and get the client safely seated before assessing.
questions.hintContent: Think about what could happen in the next few seconds.
questions.hintStrategy: When an immediate injury risk exists, safety actions come before data collection.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: An unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) reports that a client who just finished a planned walk said, “My chest feels tight.” The client is now resting in bed. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the UAP to obtain vital signs and report the results.
Go to the client's room to assess the client right away.
Tell the UAP to have the client rest and walk again later.
Document the report and recheck the client at the next round.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A new chest symptom requires the nurse's own assessment, which cannot be delegated.
Correct. New chest tightness after exertion is a potentially unstable finding the nurse must assess personally.
Incorrect. Planning more activity before assessment ignores a possible cardiac symptom.
Incorrect. Delaying assessment of a new chest symptom is unsafe.
questions.rationale: New chest discomfort related to activity calls for stopping and prompt assessment, and assessing a potentially unstable client is not delegated to a UAP. The nurse goes to the client right away to assess symptoms, vital signs, and other findings and then notifies the provider as indicated. Having the UAP take vital signs is the tempting answer because vital signs are within UAP scope, but numbers alone do not replace the nurse's assessment of a new chest symptom. Planning another walk or waiting until the next round both delay care.
questions.takeaway: New exertional chest symptoms require the RN's own prompt assessment.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether this finding could signal an unstable condition.
questions.hintStrategy: Delegate stable, routine tasks; keep assessment of new or unstable findings for the RN.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 31-year-old client at 28 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy calls the clinic. She jogs four days a week and says, “After my run this morning, I noticed some vaginal bleeding.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Advise her to stop exercising and come in today for evaluation.
Advise her to switch to walking until her next scheduled prenatal visit.
Reassure her that light spotting after exercise is expected.
Ask her to record how long and how far she ran this morning.
optionRationales: Correct. Bleeding is a possible pregnancy complication that requires stopping activity and prompt obstetric evaluation.
Incorrect. Changing the activity does not address a possible complication that needs evaluation.
Incorrect. Bleeding should not be normalized during pregnancy without evaluation.
Incorrect. Exercise details can be gathered later; the bleeding needs prompt evaluation first.
questions.rationale: Activity during pregnancy requires attention to complications and coordination with the obstetric team. Vaginal bleeding is a warning sign that requires stopping exercise and prompt evaluation, regardless of how routine her exercise has been. Switching to walking is tempting because walking is lower intensity, but it treats the bleeding as an exercise-intensity problem rather than a possible complication. Reassurance and gathering run details both delay needed assessment.
questions.takeaway: A warning sign during pregnancy means stop activity and arrange prompt obstetric evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the problem is the exercise itself or a sign that needs evaluation.
questions.hintStrategy: When a symptom could indicate a complication, choose the option that leads to evaluation now.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: On the second day after abdominal surgery, a 62-year-old client says, “I want to walk the whole hallway three times today so I can get strong fast.” The client has not yet walked since surgery. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to walk the full hallway with standby help.
Assess vital signs, pain, and dizziness when the client stands.
Explain that walking should wait until the client is discharged.
Ask the UAP to walk the client to the end of the hall and back.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The goal exceeds what has been established as safe for a client who has not yet walked.
Correct. Baseline tolerance must be assessed before a deconditioned client begins walking.
Incorrect. Early mobility is generally encouraged; the issue is a safe starting point.
Incorrect. The first postoperative walk requires nursing assessment of tolerance.
questions.rationale: After illness or surgery, activity begins with an assessed baseline and progresses gradually. This client has not walked since surgery, so the nurse first assesses vital signs, pain, and orthostatic symptoms and then plans a short supervised walk. Encouraging the full hallway is tempting because the client is motivated, but motivation does not establish tolerance. Delaying walking until discharge or delegating the first walk would also be inappropriate.
questions.takeaway: Assess tolerance before the first walk; motivation is not a safety assessment.
questions.hintContent: Ask what the nurse does not yet know about this client's tolerance.
questions.hintStrategy: When the client's ability is unknown, assess before implementing.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A 27-year-old client with paraplegia who uses a manual wheelchair asks the nurse, “Is there any exercise I can actually do?” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Explain that exercise will need to wait until a walking program is possible.
Recommend a standard gym program focused on lower-body machines.
Ask about the client's current abilities, interests, and any restrictions.
Give the client a list of local wheelchair sports teams to contact.
optionRationales: Incorrect. People with disabilities can be active as abilities allow; walking is not required.
Incorrect. This ignores the client's abilities and does not start from an assessment.
Correct. An adapted plan starts with assessing function, preferences, equipment, and the care plan.
Incorrect. Adaptive sports may fit later, but a resource list before assessment may not match the client.
questions.rationale: People with chronic conditions or disability should be as active as their abilities allow, with plans adapted to function and the care plan. The first step is assessing what the client can do, enjoys, and is restricted from, along with equipment needs. Offering a list of wheelchair sports teams is tempting because it is encouraging and specific, but it skips assessment and may not match the client's interests or ability. Saying exercise must wait for walking is inaccurate.
questions.takeaway: Disability does not rule out exercise; assess abilities and interests to adapt the plan.
questions.hintContent: Consider what information the nurse needs to individualize the plan.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before recommending; resource lists and programs come after you know the client.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 50-year-old client tells the clinic nurse he plans to begin a high-intensity interval class tomorrow. His blood pressure today is 178/104 mm Hg, and he says he ran out of his antihypertensive two weeks ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Teach him to use the talk test to keep intervals at a moderate level.
Recommend that he start with a beginner aerobics class at the gym instead.
Notify the provider and advise him to delay the class until reviewed.
Help him write a SMART goal for attending the class twice a week.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Intensity teaching does not address uncontrolled blood pressure that needs evaluation.
Incorrect. A lower-intensity class still begins exercise before the uncontrolled blood pressure is addressed.
Correct. Uncontrolled blood pressure after missed medication requires provider review before vigorous exercise.
Incorrect. Goal-setting is premature when his current condition is unstable.
questions.rationale: Interval training alternates greater and lesser effort and is not automatically appropriate for a beginner or a medically unstable person. A blood pressure of 178/104 mm Hg after two weeks without medication is uncontrolled and needs provider review before vigorous exercise. Recommending a beginner class instead is tempting because it seems like a safer compromise, but it still adds exertion before the unstable condition is addressed. Goal-setting and talk-test teaching can follow once he is cleared.
questions.takeaway: Review unstable illness with the provider before starting or advancing exercise.
questions.hintContent: Look at the vital sign and the medication history together.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client's condition is unstable, choose the option that involves the provider before any plan proceeds.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A 73-year-old client using resistance bands for shoulder strengthening reports a sharp pain in the right shoulder during the third set. The client says, “No pain, no gain, right?” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stop the exercise and assess the client's right shoulder.
Switch the client to a lighter band and finish the set.
Explain that muscle soreness is a normal response to training.
Apply ice to the shoulder and resume exercise in 15 minutes.
optionRationales: Correct. Sharp pain during exercise calls for stopping and assessing for injury.
Incorrect. Continuing before assessing sharp pain risks further injury.
Incorrect. Sharp pain during exercise is not the same as expected muscle fatigue.
Incorrect. Planning to resume before assessment ignores a possible injury.
questions.rationale: Pain is not proof that exercise is working, and sharp pain during resistance work may signal injury. The nurse stops the activity and assesses the shoulder before deciding whether, how, or when to continue. Switching to a lighter band is tempting because it reduces the load, but it continues exercise without knowing what caused the pain. The client's ‘no pain, no gain’ belief also needs teaching once the shoulder has been assessed.
questions.takeaway: Sharp pain during exercise means stop and assess; pain is not proof the exercise is working.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish expected effort from a sign of possible injury.
questions.hintStrategy: When a symptom may signal harm, choose ‘stop and assess’ over modifications that continue activity.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A home health nurse reviews activity logs submitted by four clients enrolled in a walking program. Which client requires the nurse's follow-up first?
options: The client who walked 10 minutes daily and reported mild leg muscle soreness.
The client who skipped two walks because of a family event.
The client who could talk but not sing while walking briskly.
The client who had to sit down on a bench because of lightheadedness.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Mild muscle soreness after new activity is expected and can be addressed routinely.
Incorrect. Missed sessions need problem-solving but do not indicate a physical risk.
Incorrect. This describes appropriate moderate intensity.
Correct. Lightheadedness requiring the client to sit is a concerning symptom that needs prompt assessment.
questions.rationale: Exercise plans should state which symptoms require stopping and whom to contact, and the nurse prioritizes reports of those symptoms. Lightheadedness severe enough that the client had to sit down suggests possible near-syncope and needs prompt follow-up. Mild muscle soreness is the tempting choice because it is a physical symptom, but it is an expected response to new activity. Talking but not singing indicates appropriate moderate intensity, and missed sessions are a planning issue.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize red-flag symptoms during activity over expected soreness or missed sessions.
questions.hintContent: Sort the reports into expected responses, planning issues, and warning signs.
questions.hintStrategy: In multi-client priority items, choose the one with a possible physiologic threat.
