questions.stem: A 68-year-old client recovered well physically after a fall three months ago and has the strength to walk. The client says, “I'd like to walk to church again, but I'm scared I'll fall.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Your strength is good, so you're ready to walk to church.”
“Tell me more about what worries you about walking there.”
“You could use a wheelchair for the trip until you feel safer.”
“Most people stop worrying about falling after a few weeks.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This dismisses the fear, which can limit activity regardless of strength.
Correct. Exploring the fear identifies specific concerns that can be addressed in the plan.
Incorrect. This may reduce activity and independence before the concern is understood.
Incorrect. This offers false reassurance without assessing the client's concern.
questions.rationale: Assessment includes confidence as well as capability; a person may have the strength to walk but fear falling after a recent injury. Exploring what worries the client can reveal specific concerns such as the route, weather, or device use that can be addressed with practice or support. Telling the client their strength is good is tempting because it is factually encouraging, but it dismisses the fear that is actually limiting activity. Reassurance and a wheelchair suggestion likewise skip assessment.
questions.takeaway: Assess confidence and fear as well as strength before planning activity.
questions.hintContent: Consider what is actually limiting this client's activity.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic communication, explore the feeling before reassuring or solving.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 60-year-old client who takes metoprolol says, “My heart rate never gets up to the target number on my watch, so I keep pushing harder.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Keep increasing your pace each time until your watch shows the target rate.”
“Your medication limits heart rate, so let the talk test guide your effort.”
“Stop taking metoprolol on exercise days so your heart rate can rise.”
“If your heart rate stays low, the exercise is not giving you any benefit.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pushing to a rate the medication blunts can cause overexertion.
Correct. Beta blockers blunt heart rate response, so perceived effort and the talk test are better guides.
Incorrect. A prescribed medication should not be stopped without the prescriber.
Incorrect. Benefit does not depend on reaching a specific heart rate number.
questions.rationale: Medication, illness, conditioning, and disability can alter the body's response to exercise. Beta blockers such as metoprolol limit the rise in heart rate, so a heart rate target may be unreachable and pushing harder to meet it risks overexertion. The talk test and how the client feels are more useful guides, and the target should be reviewed with the provider. Telling the client the exercise gives no benefit is the tempting misconception, but benefit does not depend on reaching one number.
questions.takeaway: When medication blunts heart rate, guide intensity by the talk test and symptoms.
questions.hintContent: Think about how a beta blocker affects heart rate during exercise.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that change a prescribed medication or encourage pushing past safe limits.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: The parent of a 9-year-old says, “She has gym class twice a week, so she gets plenty of exercise. At home she mostly plays video games.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Two gym classes a week meet the activity recommendation for her age.”
“She should start a structured weight-lifting program after school.”
“Children her age need about an hour of active play every day.”
“Limiting video games will be enough to meet her activity needs.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Children need about 60 minutes of activity daily, not two sessions a week.
Incorrect. Children benefit most from enjoyable, developmentally appropriate play.
Correct. School-age children need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily.
Incorrect. Reducing screen time alone does not ensure active play.
questions.rationale: School-age children and adolescents need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activities. Two gym classes a week fall well short of that, so the nurse explains the daily target and can explore enjoyable, developmentally appropriate activities. A structured weight program is tempting because strengthening is part of the guideline, but for children it comes mainly through active play such as climbing and jumping. Simply limiting screen time does not guarantee activity.
questions.takeaway: School-age children need about 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.
questions.hintContent: Recall the activity guideline for school-age children and whether it is daily or weekly.
questions.hintStrategy: Lifespan items: match the recommendation to the specific age group in the stem.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old client says, “I walk briskly for 25 minutes six days a week, so I'm meeting all the activity guidelines.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “You need to walk 150 minutes every day to meet the guideline.”
“That meets the aerobic goal; also add muscle strengthening 2 days a week.”
“Brisk walking does not count toward the adult activity guideline.”
“You are meeting all of the guidelines, so no further changes are needed at all.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The guideline is a weekly total, not a daily amount.
Correct. 150 minutes of moderate activity meets the aerobic target, but adults also need muscle strengthening on at least 2 days.
Incorrect. Brisk walking is a common moderate-intensity aerobic activity.
Incorrect. Aerobic minutes alone do not meet the muscle-strengthening recommendation.
questions.rationale: Adults are advised to get 150–300 minutes of moderate activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days. Twenty-five minutes on six days equals 150 minutes of moderate activity, which meets the aerobic target. Agreeing that all guidelines are met is the tempting answer because the math works, but it overlooks the muscle-strengthening component. The nurse affirms the walking and adds the missing piece.
questions.takeaway: Adult guidelines include weekly aerobic minutes plus muscle strengthening on at least 2 days.
questions.hintContent: Do the weekly math, then check whether every part of the guideline is addressed.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client says ‘all,’ check whether any component of the recommendation is missing.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A nurse is documenting a deconditioned client's response to a hallway walk. Which entry best evaluates the client's activity tolerance?
options: “Client tolerated the hallway walk well today and was encouraged to continue.”
“Walked 40 ft with walker, 1 rest; HR at baseline in 4 min; no dizziness.”
“Client walked in the hallway per the plan of care this afternoon.”
“Client states that walking is important for regaining strength.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. ‘Tolerated well’ is vague and does not describe the observed response.
Correct. This records distance, assistance, rest, recovery, and symptoms, which together show tolerance.
Incorrect. This states that walking occurred but not how the client responded.
Incorrect. A statement about importance does not describe the physiologic response.
questions.rationale: Activity tolerance is the ability to complete activity with an acceptable physiologic response and manageable symptoms. A useful evaluation records what was performed, the assistance needed, and the response, including recovery time and symptoms. Phrases such as ‘tolerated well’ are tempting because they are common in charting, but they do not tell the next nurse what the client could do or how they responded. Statements about the plan or the client's beliefs are not evaluation of tolerance.
questions.takeaway: Document distance, assistance, symptoms, and recovery, not ‘tolerated well.’
questions.hintContent: Look for the entry another nurse could use to decide whether to progress activity.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, choose specific, observable, measurable data over vague summaries.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 35-year-old client without health problems runs three times a week for 25 minutes and says, “When I'm running, I can only get out a few words before I need a breath.” The client asks whether this is enough exercise. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “That sounds like moderate intensity, so you need 150 minutes weekly.”
“That sounds like light intensity, so increase your pace when you run.”
“You need to run every day of the week to get the full benefit from it.”
“That is vigorous intensity; 75 minutes a week meets the aerobic goal.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Speaking only a few words indicates vigorous, not moderate, intensity.
Incorrect. Being limited to a few words reflects vigorous effort, not light.
Incorrect. The guideline is a weekly total, and daily running is not required.
Correct. Saying only a few words indicates vigorous effort, and 75 vigorous minutes meets the minimum weekly aerobic target.
questions.rationale: In the talk test, a person at moderate intensity can talk but not sing, while at vigorous intensity they can say only a few words before pausing for breath. This client's running is vigorous, and three 25-minute sessions total 75 minutes, which meets the minimum vigorous aerobic target for adults. Classifying it as moderate is the tempting error, which would lead to telling the client they are only halfway to 150 minutes. Muscle strengthening on two days a week should still be addressed.
questions.takeaway: Only a few words before a breath means vigorous intensity; 75 vigorous minutes weekly meets the aerobic minimum.
questions.hintContent: Use the talk test to identify the intensity, then do the weekly math.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the category first (intensity), then apply the rule for that category.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A client with depression who is starting outpatient treatment asks, “Will exercise help me at all?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Activity can help mood, stress, and sleep alongside your treatment.”
“Exercise will cure depression if you do it every day for a month.”
“Exercise mainly benefits the heart, so it will not affect your mood.”
“If you exercise enough, you may be able to stop your medication.”
optionRationales: Correct. Activity has psychosocial benefits and supports, rather than replaces, treatment.
Incorrect. Nurses should not promise that exercise cures a chronic condition.
Incorrect. Psychosocial benefits include improved mood, reduced stress, and better sleep.
Incorrect. This suggests changing prescribed treatment and overstates the benefit.
questions.rationale: Regular activity supports emotional, social, and cognitive wellness through improved mood, reduced stress, better sleep, and chances for connection. The nurse describes these benefits accurately as part of the overall treatment plan. Promising a cure is the tempting overstatement, because the benefits are real, but exercise does not guarantee recovery from a chronic condition. Suggesting the client could stop medication would encourage an unsafe, unsupervised change.
questions.takeaway: Exercise has real psychosocial benefits, but do not promise it cures disease or replaces treatment.
questions.hintContent: Look for the response that is accurate without overpromising.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options with guarantees (‘will cure’) or suggestions to change prescribed therapy.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client with osteoarthritis says, “What I really want is to get back to working in my vegetable garden.” Which plan element best connects the activity plan to the client's goal?
options: Walking on a treadmill for 30 minutes on five days a week.
Practicing sit-to-stand and carrying a light watering can.
Losing 10 pounds before returning to any gardening tasks.
Joining a high-intensity group exercise class at a local gym.
optionRationales: Incorrect. This builds endurance but does not target the movements gardening requires.
Correct. Functional practice of gardening movements links the exercise to the client's valued task.
Incorrect. Weight is not the client's goal, and delaying gardening reduces meaningful participation.
Incorrect. A demanding class may not fit the client's ability, joints, or goal.
questions.rationale: A functional goal turns an abstract recommendation into something the client values, which supports motivation and participation. Gardening requires getting up and down, carrying, and balance, so practicing sit-to-stand and carrying a light watering can builds the specific abilities the client needs. Treadmill walking is tempting because it is a standard endurance activity, but it does not address the movements of the task the client cares about. Requiring weight loss first shifts the goal away from the client's priority.
questions.takeaway: Link activity to the client's valued functional goal.
questions.hintContent: Consider what movements the client's goal actually requires.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that is individualized to the client's stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 22-year-old client has a long leg cast after a tibia fracture and wants to keep the thigh muscles strong while the knee is immobilized. Which exercise should the nurse expect to teach?
options: Bending and straightening the knee against light resistance.
Tightening and holding the thigh muscle without moving the knee.
Riding a stationary bicycle at a slow, comfortable pace.
Climbing stairs slowly at home while holding onto the handrail.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The knee is immobilized in the cast and cannot move through range.
Correct. Isometric contraction builds tension without joint movement, which fits an immobilized knee.
Incorrect. Cycling requires knee movement, which the cast prevents.
Incorrect. Stair climbing is isotonic and requires knee flexion and extension.
questions.rationale: Isometric exercise creates muscle tension while the joint remains still, so it can maintain strength when a joint is immobilized. Tightening and holding the thigh muscle within the cast fits that description. Light-resistance knee bending is tempting because it is a common strengthening exercise, but it is isotonic and requires joint movement the cast prevents. The nurse also teaches the client to keep breathing during each contraction to avoid a Valsalva-related rise in blood pressure.
questions.takeaway: When a joint cannot move, isometric contractions maintain muscle strength.
questions.hintContent: Decide which exercises require the knee joint to move.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify by mechanism: joint movement (isotonic) versus no joint movement (isometric).

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a community group of adults about the benefits of regular physical activity. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Regular activity can improve your mood and help you sleep better.”
“Weight-bearing and strength activities help keep your bones strong.”
“Being active can help manage blood pressure and blood glucose.”
“Exercising regularly will prevent you from developing any disease.”
“Balance and strength activities can help you stay independent.”
“If you already have arthritis, regular exercise will cure it.”
optionRationales: Correct. Psychosocial benefits include improved mood, reduced stress, and better sleep.
Correct. Activity supports bone strength.
Correct. Regular activity supports blood pressure and glucose management.
Incorrect. Nurses should not promise that exercise prevents every disease.
Correct. Improved strength, balance, and mobility support independence.
Incorrect. Exercise can improve function but does not cure chronic conditions.
questions.rationale: Regular activity can improve endurance, strength, balance, and mobility; support blood pressure, glucose, and bone health; and improve mood, stress, and sleep. These benefits connect physical fitness with emotional, social, and functional wellness. Statements promising to prevent every disease or cure a chronic condition overstate the evidence and set clients up for disappointment. The ‘prevent any disease’ statement is tempting because activity lowers many risks, but lowering risk is not a guarantee.
questions.takeaway: Teach the real benefits of activity without promising prevention of all disease or cure.
questions.hintContent: Watch for statements that turn ‘can help’ into a guarantee.
questions.hintStrategy: Absolute words such as ‘any’ and ‘will cure’ usually signal an incorrect option.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: After a knee arthroscopy, a client's surgeon allows only exercises that do not move the knee joint this week. Which exercises are appropriate for the nurse to reinforce? Select all that apply.
options: Tightening the front thigh muscle while the knee stays straight.
Squeezing the buttock muscles together and holding for a few seconds.
Pressing the heel down into the bed without bending the knee.
Performing mini squats while holding onto a kitchen counter.
Pedaling a stationary bicycle at a slow pace for 10 minutes.
Lifting an ankle weight by straightening the knee while seated.
optionRationales: Correct. A quadriceps set is isometric and produces tension without knee movement.
Correct. A gluteal set is isometric and does not move the knee.
Correct. This hamstring set produces tension without knee joint movement.
Incorrect. Squats bend the knee, which is isotonic movement.
Incorrect. Cycling moves the knee through flexion and extension.
Incorrect. Seated knee extension moves the knee joint against resistance.
questions.rationale: Isometric exercise produces muscle tension without appreciable joint movement, which matches a restriction against moving the knee. Quadriceps sets, gluteal sets, and pressing the heel into the bed all build tension while the knee stays still. Mini squats, cycling, and seated knee extensions are isotonic because the muscle changes length and the knee moves. Stationary cycling is tempting because it seems gentle, but gentleness does not change the fact that the knee bends.
questions.takeaway: No joint movement allowed means isometric exercises only.
questions.hintContent: For each exercise, picture whether the knee bends or straightens.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify by mechanism, not by how gentle or intense the exercise seems.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client asks for help starting an exercise routine. Which information should the nurse gather before making a recommendation? Select all that apply.
options: Falls in the past year and any fear of falling.
Current medications and any activity restrictions.
Activities the client enjoys or has done in the past.
Safe, affordable places the client can be active.
The national weekly minute target the client should start at.
Whether the client's weight is above ideal to decide if exercise is needed.
optionRationales: Correct. Fall history and confidence affect safe activity choices.
Correct. Medications and restrictions may change the safe plan or the client's response.
Correct. Preferences support participation and adherence.
Correct. Cost, access, and environment determine whether the plan is feasible.
Incorrect. Population targets are not individual starting doses.
Incorrect. Activity benefits everyone; weight alone does not determine the need for exercise.
questions.rationale: Before recommending activity, the nurse assesses usual activity, symptoms, falls, devices, medications, restrictions, preferences, and access. Fall history and fear, medications and restrictions, enjoyment, and safe affordable locations all shape a plan the client can safely carry out. A national weekly target is tempting because it is evidence-based, but it describes population goals rather than an individual starting point. Using weight to decide whether exercise is needed ignores the many benefits of activity unrelated to weight.
questions.takeaway: Assess safety, restrictions, preferences, and access before recommending activity.
questions.hintContent: Ask which data would change what the nurse recommends for this person.
questions.hintStrategy: In assessment SATA items, select data specific to the client; reject general rules.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A nurse is assigning care for a stable client whose plan includes walking in the hallway three times a day with standby assistance. Which tasks can the nurse delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)? Select all that apply.
options: Walking with the client in the hallway according to the plan.
Recording the distance the client walks each time.
Stopping the walk and reporting if the client becomes dizzy.
Teaching the client a new technique for using the walker.
Deciding whether the client is ready to walk a longer distance.
optionRationales: Correct. Ambulating a stable client per an established plan is within UAP scope.
Correct. Measuring and recording data is within UAP scope.
Correct. UAP can stop activity and report findings for the nurse to assess.
Incorrect. Teaching requires nursing judgment and is not delegated to UAP.
Incorrect. Evaluating tolerance and progressing activity require nursing judgment.
questions.rationale: UAP can carry out routine tasks for stable clients, such as ambulating per an established plan and recording measurable data. They should be told which findings require stopping the activity and reporting to the nurse. Teaching new skills and deciding whether to progress activity require assessment and evaluation, which remain with the RN. Teaching walker technique is tempting to delegate because it seems simple, but teaching is outside UAP scope.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine ambulation and data collection; keep teaching and evaluation with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Sort tasks into ‘doing and reporting’ versus ‘judging and teaching.’
questions.hintStrategy: UAP cannot assess, teach, evaluate, or care for unstable clients; check each option against that rule.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with no activity restrictions is independent and walks daily. Which recommendations are appropriate for the nurse to include in the activity plan? Select all that apply.
options: Continue aerobic activity toward adult weekly targets as abilities allow.
Add balance activities such as standing on one foot near a counter.
Include muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week.
Avoid all strength training because of the risk of injury with age.
Practice functional tasks such as rising from a chair without using the arms.
Limit walking to 10 minutes a week to prevent overexertion.
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults follow adult aerobic guidelines as abilities allow.
Correct. Balance training is a recommended addition for older adults.
Correct. Muscle strengthening on 2 or more days is recommended for older adults.
Incorrect. Age alone is not a reason to avoid strength training; it supports function.
Correct. Functional activity supports independence in daily tasks.
Incorrect. An arbitrary limit undercuts the activity of an independent, active client.
questions.rationale: Older adults follow adult activity recommendations as abilities allow and add balance and functional activities. This active, independent client can continue aerobic activity, add balance and functional training, and do muscle strengthening on at least two days. Avoiding strength training because of age is the tempting misconception, but strength supports bones, function, and independence. Arbitrarily limiting walking would reduce fitness in a client with no restrictions.
questions.takeaway: Older adults: adult aerobic targets as able, plus balance, strength, and functional activity.
questions.hintContent: Recall what is added to adult recommendations for older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Be cautious of options that restrict activity based on age alone.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: Three weeks ago, a deconditioned 69-year-old client began a walking plan after a hospital stay. Which findings at today's follow-up indicate progress toward the client's goal? Select all that apply.
options: The client now walks 10 minutes without stopping, up from 3 minutes.
The client's breathing returns to normal more quickly after walking.
The client can now carry a bag of groceries from the car.
The client's body weight is unchanged from three weeks ago.
The client reports new ankle pain that wakes them at night.
The client says, “I feel more confident going out on my own.”
optionRationales: Correct. Increased duration shows improved endurance from the baseline.
Correct. Faster recovery is evidence of improved activity tolerance.
Correct. Improved performance of a valued task shows functional progress.
Incorrect. Unchanged weight does not indicate progress, and progress can occur without weight change.
Incorrect. New pain is a concern that requires assessment, not a sign of progress.
Correct. Increased confidence and participation are meaningful outcomes.
questions.rationale: Evaluation compares actual performance with the baseline and the goal, including endurance, recovery, function, confidence, and safety. Longer walking time, faster recovery, carrying groceries, and greater confidence all show progress even if body weight has not changed. New night-time ankle pain is a concern to assess. Unchanged weight is tempting to read as lack of progress, but weight is not the only outcome and was not the goal of this plan.
questions.takeaway: Measure progress by endurance, recovery, function, and confidence, not weight alone.
questions.hintContent: Compare each finding with where the client started three weeks ago.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluate-outcome SATA items, select findings that show improvement toward the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a 45-year-old client who is starting a home exercise program after being sedentary. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Begin each session with a few minutes of gentle warm-up.”
“Wear supportive shoes that fit well and suit the activity.”
“Increase the time or intensity gradually over several weeks.”
“Push through pain, because it shows the workout is effective.”
“Hold your breath during each lift to keep your core stable.”
“Stop and get medical help right away if you have new chest discomfort.”
optionRationales: Correct. Warm-up prepares muscles and the cardiovascular system for activity.
Correct. Appropriate footwear reduces injury risk.
Correct. Gradual progression lowers injury and overexertion risk.
Incorrect. Pain is not proof that exercise is working and may signal injury.
Incorrect. Breath-holding can raise blood pressure sharply; clients should keep breathing.
Correct. The plan should state which symptoms require stopping and whom to contact.
questions.rationale: Safe exercise teaching includes warm-up, appropriate equipment and footwear, gradual progression, and clear instructions about which symptoms require stopping and whom to contact. Pain is not proof that exercise is working, and breath-holding during exertion can raise blood pressure sharply through the Valsalva effect. The breath-holding instruction is tempting because core bracing is common advice, but clients should keep breathing during contractions. New chest discomfort is a stop-and-report symptom.
questions.takeaway: Teach warm-up, proper footwear, gradual progression, normal breathing, and when to stop.
questions.hintContent: Look for instructions that could cause injury or a blood pressure spike.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each instruction independently for safety; reject ‘push through’ advice.
questions.ref: Module 7 · Exemplar 7.A Physical Fitness & Exercise · slides 38–49
